summary: Describes how to make DNSSEC NSEC records that cover a smaller range of names than RFC 4034 calls for. Generated and signed on demand, they let servers stop others from listing a zone's contents by walking the NSEC chain. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of a signed note listing every name on the street, the server writes a tiny note on demand that says only that nothing is here, so nobody learns the neighbors.

questions: how to prevent nsec zone walking
what is on-line signing in dnssec
subtitle: Signing tiny, on-demand NSEC records so DNSSEC zones cannot be listed by zone walking.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC NSEC records list the next existing name in a zone, so repeated queries let anyone walk the chain and retrieve every name, even where zone transfers are forbidden.
tldr.mechanism: The server makes NSEC records that cover as few names as possible, generating and signing some on demand, so walking takes about as many queries as guessing every possible name.
tldr.outcome: Zone walking becomes impractical, but the server needs its private keys online, which adds risks. The RFC notes that the NSEC3 mechanism was being worked on as an alternative.

facts.label: Maximum label length used in decrement

today: RFC 4470 is a Proposed Standard from April 2006 that updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself points to NSEC3 as a mechanism then under development that avoids on-line signing.

sections.title: The Zone-Walking Problem
sections.content:
With DNSSEC, an NSEC record lists the next existing name in its zone, proving that no names exist in the span between its owner name and its next name. The record is said to cover that span.

By querying repeatedly and following the NSEC records, anyone can retrieve every name in the zone. This is called walking the zone. Some zone owners forbid zone transfers to arbitrary clients, and this side effect of NSEC undermines that policy.

This RFC updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. It builds NSEC records that cover fewer names, so that walking takes about as many queries as asking for all possible names.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed list that says which name comes next lets a snoop follow the list from door to door and learn every name.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
The technique suits a zone owner who wants DNSSEC, worries about exposing zone contents through walking, and will bear the cost of on-line signing. That means private keys are available to the servers, with an increased chance of key disclosure and a greater exposure to denial of service.

The RFC adds that the DNSEXT working group was then working on a mechanism, tentatively called NSEC3, that prevents walking without on-line signing. It would likely reveal slightly more about the zone, such as the number of names, but could be preferable.
sections.plainLanguage: This trick is for someone who really wants to keep the neighbors secret and does not mind extra work and risk.

sections.title: Minimally Covering NSEC Records
sections.content:
There are two changes. First, in the NSEC record of an existing name, the next name field may hold any name that falls after the owner name and before the next existing name, in the ordering of RFC 4034 Section 6.1. These records can still be signed ahead of time and are returned when proving something about that exact name. This relaxes the rule that the field holds the next owner name.

Second, whenever a name must be proven not to exist, the server makes and signs a new NSEC record on demand. Its owner name falls after any existing name and before the queried name (QNAME), and its next name falls after the QNAME but before any existing name.

The generated record's type bitmap MUST have the RRSIG and NSEC bits set and SHOULD NOT have any others. Each generated record MUST have RRSIGs for each algorithm in the zone's DNSKEY set. Limiting the number of algorithms reduces the signatures needed.

A record denying a wildcard can be made the same way, and servers may pregenerate or cache it since many queries use it.
sections.plainLanguage: When asked about a missing house, the server draws a tiny gap just around that house, signs it, and says nothing lives in the gap.

sections.title: Epsilon Functions
sections.content:
The functions that produce the nearby names are called epsilon functions. They need not be perfect or consistent, but generated NSEC records must not cover any existing name, and the technique works best when records cover as few names as possible. The RFC does not define perfect functions but gives ones that come close.

  • To increment a name, add a leading label with a single null (zero-value) octet.
  • To decrement a name, decrement the last character of the leftmost label, then fill that label to 63 octets with octets of value 255.

Both functions ignore limits on the number of labels and total name length. A server must therefore check whether any existing names fall inside the generated span. If so, it substitutes the existing owner name for the NSEC owner name or next name. If an existing name is used as the owner, its real NSEC record MUST be returned.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the spot just after a name, add the tiniest possible bit. To find the spot just before it, back up by one tiny step.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content: For an A query at the non-existent name example.com, the RFC shows two generated NSEC records: one denying the name itself and one denying a wildcard. Before answering, the server tests for existing names between the endpoints. If one such as exampldd.com exists, a better epsilon function may be used, or the covered name closest to the QNAME may be the NSEC owner name or next name.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks that its small gap does not accidentally hide a real house, and shrinks the gap if it does.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On-demand signing creates three risks. Authoritative servers need access to the zone's private keys, and keeping them on well-known Internet-accessible servers makes disclosure more likely. Signing is computationally demanding, so the servers are open to denial of service. If the epsilon functions are predictable, on-demand signing may allow a chosen-plaintext attack on the private keys, so zones should use algorithms resistant to such attacks.

The anti-walking value depends on the quality of the epsilon functions. A name obviously derived from the next existing name is easily reversed, and one that stays close to it is a poor choice. The best choices produce the immediately following and preceding names.

Replay of an old NSEC record after a name was added in its span is a danger that already exists in DNSSEC. The smaller spans here actually reduce it.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping the signing stamp where the server can reach it all the time is riskier, and if the gaps are easy to guess, the secret leaks anyway.
